images.title: One cup too many
images.purpose: Show that three cups of 1/3 fill one glass exactly, so a fourth cup of 1/3 takes four thirds past one glass: 4/3 > 1.
images.composition: One tall full glass on the left, a plus sign, and one small cup on the right, with one short inequality centred below.
images.exact_structure: Left: one tall straight-sided glass split by 2 thin grey #6B7280 lines into exactly 3 equal parts, all 3 filled teal #0072B2 to the brim. Centre: a plain plus sign. Right: one small straight-sided cup, exactly as wide as the glass and exactly one third of its height, filled amber #E69F00. Below, centred: one line of text in reddish purple #CC79A7. Exactly 1 glass, 1 cup.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
a glass that is not full, or a cup not one third of the glass
images.takeaway: Three thirds already make one whole, so four thirds is more than one.
images.description: A full glass of 3 equal thirds labelled 3/3 = 1, plus one extra cup of 1/3; below, 4/3 > 1.
images.context: Shown with the concept as its one key picture, next to the walkthrough video. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not generated yet.
images.teaching_notes: Ask the student to point at the full glass and say where the extra cup would have to go.

image_decisions.why: A full glass plus one extra cup makes the reason four thirds exceeds one visible at once.
